Explain how parallel processing and multi-core processors increase throughput and why the gains are limited. That is the heart of it.

The simple Von Neumann machine fetches and executes one instruction at a time, from one memory, over one shared set of buses. For decades performance grew mainly by raising the clock speed, but faster clocks use more power and produce more heat, and beyond a certain point a chip cannot be cooled cheaply or run from a battery for long. Designers therefore look for other ways to get more work done every second, and the alternative architectures in this lesson each tackle a different limit. Parallel processing, multi-core processors and graphics processing units carry out many operations at the same time.
Makes sense. Keep going.

The Harvard architecture removes the bottleneck of a shared memory bus by giving instructions and data separate paths. Reduced instruction set computers simplify the instructions themselves so that each one finishes quickly and the pipeline keeps flowing, using less power. Real devices mix these ideas: a smartphone chip typically combines several RISC cores, a GPU and other co-processors, with separate instruction and data caches inside each core. Understanding the strengths and limits of each approach lets you explain why a games console, an office PC, a smartwatch and a washing machine contain such different processors, and choose a suitable design for a given job.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Parallel processing means using two or more processors or cores to work on different parts of a task at the same time. A multi-core processor places several complete cores on one chip, each with its own control unit, ALU, registers and level 1 cache, usually sharing a larger level 3 cache. The operating system schedules programs, or threads within a program, onto the cores so they run simultaneously, which improves multitasking and speeds up software written to divide its work. Gains depend on how much of a task can be split. Any part that must run in order, because each step needs the result of the one before, still runs on a single core, so it sets a floor on the total time.
Got it. Keep going.

If a job takes 100 seconds and 20 of those seconds are sequential, no number of cores can bring it below 20 seconds. On top of this, dividing the work, keeping the cores coordinated and combining results all take time, and cores compete for shared cache, memory and bus. That is why a quad-core processor rarely runs a program four times faster. Parallel systems also need operating systems and programs that are written to use threads, which makes them harder to develop and test.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

In the Von Neumann architecture, instructions and data share one memory and one set of buses, so they must be fetched one after the other, and the processor can be left waiting: the Von Neumann bottleneck. Its advantages are simplicity, lower cost and flexibility, since any part of memory can hold either a program or data, which suits general-purpose computers that run many different programs. The Harvard architecture uses physically separate memories and buses for instructions and for data. The processor can therefore fetch the next instruction while reading or writing data, improving speed and making timing predictable.
Okay. Keep going.

The two memories can also be built differently: the instruction memory can be non-volatile flash of one word length, and the data memory a small amount of RAM of another. The drawbacks are extra complexity and less flexibility, because spare instruction memory cannot be used to hold data. Harvard designs are common in embedded systems, the dedicated computers inside devices such as heating controllers, car braking systems and card readers, and in digital signal processors that handle audio and video streams. Modern PCs use a hybrid: main memory follows Von Neumann, but each core has separate level 1 caches for instructions and for data.
Go on.

Every processor has an instruction set, the complete set of machine-code operations it can carry out. A complex instruction set computer provides a large number of instructions, some of which perform several low-level steps in one go, such as reading two values from memory, multiplying them and storing the answer. Instructions vary in length and may take several clock cycles. CISC designs date from a time when memory was expensive and compilers were simple, so packing more work into each instruction kept programs small. A reduced instruction set computer provides a smaller set of simple, fixed-length instructions, most completing in a single clock cycle, with only load and store instructions accessing memory and everything else working on registers.
Right. Keep going.

A RISC program needs more instructions for the same task, and the compiler does more of the work, but the hardware is simpler. Simpler circuits use fewer transistors, consume less power and produce less heat, and uniform instructions keep a pipeline full. This is why ARM processors, which are RISC, dominate phones and tablets and now appear in many laptops, while x86 processors from Intel and AMD, which are CISC, remain common in desktop PCs largely because of compatibility with existing software. Internally, modern x86 chips break complex instructions into simpler RISC-like steps.
Go on.

A co-processor is an additional processor that takes over a particular type of work from the main CPU. The most important is the graphics processing unit. A CPU has a small number of powerful cores with large caches and complex control logic, designed to handle varied, sequential tasks full of decisions. A GPU instead has hundreds or thousands of simpler cores that apply the same instruction to many items of data at once, an approach called SIMD, single instruction, multiple data. Graphics fits this perfectly: to draw a frame, the same lighting or colour calculation must be carried out for millions of pixels, and each pixel can be worked out independently.
Makes sense. Keep going.

The same strength makes GPUs valuable outside graphics. Training machine-learning models involves enormous numbers of identical multiplications on large arrays of numbers, and video encoding, cryptography, weather forecasting and scientific simulations have similar patterns. GPU performance is often quoted in FLOPS, floating-point operations per second. GPUs are poor at sequential, branching work, so they cannot replace the CPU, which still runs the operating system and coordinates everything. Phone chips also contain other co-processors, such as image signal processors and neural engines, each optimised for one kind of task while using little power.
Go on.

No single design is best for everything; the right choice depends on what the device must do, how much power it can use, how much it can cost and what software it must run. A fitness tracker or smartwatch needs to run for days on a tiny battery, so a low-power RISC microcontroller, often using a Harvard-style memory arrangement, is ideal. A washing machine or heating controller runs one fixed program that must respond reliably to sensors, which suits an inexpensive Harvard microcontroller with its program in flash memory. An office PC must run a wide range of existing Windows applications, so a multi-core x86 processor with Von Neumann main memory remains the usual choice, although ARM-based laptops now offer longer battery life.
Got it. Keep going.

A smartphone combines multi-core RISC processing with a built-in GPU and other co-processors to give smooth graphics and long battery life without a fan. Training an artificial intelligence model or running a weather simulation needs vast numbers of identical calculations, so GPUs or large many-core parallel systems are used. When evaluating, weigh speed for the actual workload, power and heat, cost, size and software compatibility, and remember that adding parallel hardware only helps when the task can be split.

What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Comparison questions reward paired points that state both sides, for example 'RISC instructions usually take one clock cycle, whereas some CISC instructions take several'. A list of facts about only one side earns little. Link each feature to a consequence: fewer transistors lead to lower power use and longer battery life; separate buses let an instruction and data be fetched at the same time. For 'describe parallel processing', mention two or more processors or cores, working simultaneously, on different parts of the same task. For limitations of more cores, give a reason such as sequential parts of a program, software not written for threads, or competition for shared memory, rather than simply saying 'it does not always help'. When explaining why a GPU is used, mention many simple cores and the same operation applied to many data items in parallel, and link this to the task in the question. Harvard questions often ask for a typical use: embedded systems, microcontrollers or digital signal processors earn credit, but 'a desktop PC' does not. Avoid absolute claims such as 'RISC is always faster' or 'more cores always doubles speed'. In extended questions, apply each point to the scenario and finish with a justified recommendation.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. A task takes 100 s on one core, and 40 s of it must run sequentially. What is the shortest time it could take with unlimited cores? Is it A, 0 s; B, 10 s; C, 40 s; D, 60 s?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: 40 s. Only the 60 s parallel part can shrink; the 40 s sequential part always remains.
